brief.question: What were the main debates in the Australian parliament in 2024, and what positions did members and parties take? Debates that year included The stage 3 tax cuts, The detention ruling, Supermarket prices and Gambling ads.
brief.answer:
The year’s parliamentary debates were dominated by cost-of-living measures, with the Treasury Laws Amendment (Cost of Living Tax Cuts) Bill 2024 a central focus. The government, led by Prime Minister Albanese, argued for revised stage 3 tax cuts to deliver help to middle Australia, with the bill reducing the lowest tax rate from 19% to 16% and delivering an average worker tax cut of over $1,500 per year. Treasurer Jim Chalmers defended the changes, accusing the opposition of preferring higher wages and inflation and wanting tax cuts skewed to the highest incomes. The Coalition, however, accused the government of lying about stage 3 tax cuts, with members like the member for Moncrieff claiming the government had broken promises on electricity prices, mortgages, and child care. The Senate passed a motion to bring on the tax cuts debate, with Liberal Senator Simon Birmingham noting the government needed Liberal and Greens support to pass the bill.

Supermarket pricing and gambling advertising also sparked significant debate. In March, crossbench members including Bob Katter and Andrew Wilkie moved to suspend standing orders to address the "Coles and Woolworths oligopoly," arguing it had an appalling impact on farmers and consumers, with Australians being overcharged punitively while farmers received below-cost prices. This motion was defeated 13–52, with Labor and most crossbenchers voting against. Later, in November, a motion to adjourn debate on gambling advertising passed 71–64, with Labor members voting in favour of the adjournment while the Coalition, Greens, and several independents voted against, indicating a split over how to proceed on restricting gambling ads. The Greens also criticised the Victorian state budget for failing to address cost-of-living crises, calling for supermarket price regulation and new taxes on big banks.

The Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Bill 2024 passed its second reading 97–6 in November, with Liberal MP Bridget Archer crossing the floor to vote against her party, joining the Greens and independents in opposition. The Future Made in Australia (Production Tax Credits and Other Measures) Bill 2024 also saw debate adjourned 73–62. Additionally, the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Accountability and Fairness) Bill 2023 passed the Senate 31–26, with Labor and the Greens supporting it while the Coalition opposed.
